items.stem: About what share of Europe's population died in the Black Death of 1347–1351?
items.answer: Between a third and a half
items.markingKey: Between a third and a half. Estimates vary by region.

items.stem: Distinguish between a lord and a serf.
items.answer: A lord held land and had rights over the people on his manor; a serf worked the lord's land, owed him labour and could not leave without permission.
items.markingKey: A lord held land and had rights over the people on his manor; a serf worked the lord's land, owed him labour and could not leave without permission. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Diego writes: "Medieval peasants never resisted their lords." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Peasants resisted through petitions, poaching and revolts such as the 1381 Peasants' Revolt and the French Jacquerie of 1358.
items.markingKey: Peasants resisted through petitions, poaching and revolts such as the 1381 Peasants' Revolt and the French Jacquerie of 1358. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A – Royal charter (paraphrased): Paraphrase of clauses 39 and 40 of Magna Carta, sealed by King John at Runnymede, June 1215

No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land. To no one will we sell, deny or delay right or justice.

What is the message of Source A about feudal society in medieval Europe? Refer to details in the source.
items.answer: The king must not punish free men without lawful judgement and must not sell or delay justice.
items.markingKey: The king must not punish free men without lawful judgement and must not sell or delay justice. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "Was the Middle Ages bad?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into feudal society in medieval Europe. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a vague value judgement covering a thousand years Improved: "How did labour shortages after the Black Death change the lives of peasants in England between 1348 and 1400?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a vague value judgement covering a thousand years); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How did labour shortages after the Black Death change the lives of peasants in England between 1348 and 1400?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The Black Death was the main reason for the decline of feudalism in England."
items.answer: An important accelerator rather than the only cause: it sped up changes in labour and money rents that had already begun.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: labour shortages raised wages and peasants' bargaining power; it led to the Statute of Labourers and the 1381 revolt. Arguments against: money rents were already replacing labour services before 1348; the growth of towns, trade and royal government also weakened feudal ties. Supported judgement: An important accelerator rather than the only cause: it sped up changes in labour and money rents that had already begun.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "One-tenth of a person's produce or income paid to the Church"?
items.answer: tithe
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of tithe.

items.stem: Explain why William I introduced a feudal system after conquering England in 1066.
items.answer: He needed to control a hostile population with a small army, so he granted land to loyal Norman nobles who built castles and provided knights, binding them to him by oaths.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: He needed to control a hostile population with a small army, so he granted land to loyal Norman nobles who built castles and provided knights, binding them to him by oaths. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How did labour shortages after the Black Death change the lives of peasants in England between 1348 and 1400?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Read two secondary accounts; examine translated sources (Statute of Labourers 1351, manor court rolls); record evidence about wages and services in a table; build a timeline; evaluate how typical the sources are.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Read two secondary accounts; examine translated sources (Statute of Labourers 1351, manor court rolls); record evidence about wages and services in a table; build a timeline; evaluate how typical the sources are. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.answer: Thesis: An important accelerator rather than the only cause: it sped up changes in labour and money rents that had already begun.

items.stem: Which emperor ruled from 1658 to 1707, when the empire reached its greatest extent?
items.answer: Aurangzeb
items.markingKey: A. Long wars in the Deccan strained the empire.

items.stem: Mei writes: "The Mughals ruled only through force." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They also used alliances (e.g. with Rajput rulers), a salaried officer corps, revenue systems and patronage of art and religion to win loyalty.
items.markingKey: They also used alliances (e.g. with Rajput rulers), a salaried officer corps, revenue systems and patronage of art and religion to win loyalty. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a zamindar and a mansabdar.
items.answer: A mansabdar was an imperial officer with a rank and salary set by the emperor; a zamindar was a local landholder with hereditary rights to collect revenue from peasants.
items.markingKey: A mansabdar was an imperial officer with a rank and salary set by the emperor; a zamindar was a local landholder with hereditary rights to collect revenue from peasants. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into the Mughal Empire: administration, culture and religion?
options: How did Akbar use marriage alliances and appointments to win the loyalty of Rajput rulers between 1562 and 1605?
items.answer: How did Akbar use marriage alliances and appointments to win the loyalty of Rajput rulers between 1562 and 1605?
items.markingKey: D. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: In which century did work begins on the Taj Mahal (approx.) (1632 CE) take place?
items.answer: 17th century CE
items.markingKey: B. 1632 CE falls in the 17th century CE: e.g. the 15th century CE runs from 1401 to 1500.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Akbar was the most successful Mughal emperor."
items.answer: Thesis: Akbar has the strongest claim because his administrative and religious policies created stability that lasted for a century, even if the empire was larger later.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: he expanded the empire and built lasting systems (mansabdari, zabt); his tolerance won the loyalty of diverse subjects. Counter-arguments: Aurangzeb ruled the largest territory; Shah Jahan's reign was a high point of wealth and architecture. Thesis/conclusion: Akbar has the strongest claim because his administrative and religious policies created stability that lasted for a century, even if the empire was larger later. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Define the term "mansabdari system".
items.answer: Akbar's system of ranks (mansabs) in which officials held a rank that fixed their pay and the number of cavalry they had to supply
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: Akbar's system of ranks (mansabs) in which officials held a rank that fixed their pay and the number of cavalry they had to supply. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.answer: a secondary source
items.markingKey: a secondary source. It interprets earlier evidence.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a primary source and a secondary source.
items.answer: A primary source comes from the time or from a witness (e.g. a diary, a law code); a secondary source is a later interpretation by someone who was not there (e.g. a textbook).
items.markingKey: A primary source comes from the time or from a witness (e.g. a diary, a law code); a secondary source is a later interpretation by someone who was not there (e.g. a textbook). items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the date of a source matters when judging its value.
items.answer: A source made at the time may record details accurately, while one written long after may rely on memory or others; but a later source may have more information and hindsight. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A source made at the time may record details accurately, while one written long after may rely on memory or others; but a later source may have more information and hindsight. items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why a biased source can still be valuable to a historian.
items.answer: It reveals the attitudes and perspective of its creator and audience – e.g. Norman propaganda shows how William justified the conquest – even if it is not a balanced account of events.
items.markingKey: Content: It reveals the attitudes and perspective of its creator and audience – e.g. Norman propaganda shows how William justified the conquest – even if it is not a balanced account of events. items.stem: Lars argues that "Historians should rely mainly on primary sources." Sana disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Historians need both: primary sources are the evidence, but secondary sources supply context and debate needed to interpret them.
items.markingKey: Lars: they are direct evidence from the time. Sana: they are often incomplete, biased or hard to interpret without context. Judgement (1-2 marks): Historians need both: primary sources are the evidence, but secondary sources supply context and debate needed to interpret them.

items.stem:
Source A – Chronicle (paraphrased): Paraphrase of William of Poitiers, "Gesta Guillelmi" (The Deeds of William), written c. 1071–1077 by William I's chaplain

The chronicler wrote that Harold had sworn an oath on holy relics to support Duke William's claim to the English throne. By taking the crown himself in January 1066, Harold had broken his oath, so William's invasion was a just war with the blessing of the Pope.

"Historians should rely mainly on primary sources." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Historians need both: primary sources are the evidence, but secondary sources supply context and debate needed to interpret them.
items.markingKey: From the source: William's invasion was justified because Harold broke a sacred oath. Own knowledge for: they are direct evidence from the time; they show contemporary perspectives and language. Own knowledge against: they are often incomplete, biased or hard to interpret without context; secondary sources bring together many primary sources and expert analysis. Judgement: Historians need both: primary sources are the evidence, but secondary sources supply context and debate needed to interpret them. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem:
Source A – Chronicle (paraphrased): Paraphrase of William of Poitiers, "Gesta Guillelmi" (The Deeds of William), written c. 1071–1077 by William I's chaplain

The chronicler wrote that Harold had sworn an oath on holy relics to support Duke William's claim to the English throne. By taking the crown himself in January 1066, Harold had broken his oath, so William's invasion was a just war with the blessing of the Pope.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into primary and secondary sources of evidence in history, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of William of Poitiers, "Gesta Guillelmi" (The Deeds of William), written c. 1071–1077 by William I's chaplain. Purpose: to justify the Norman Conquest and praise William. Value: Written close to the events by someone at William's court, it shows the Norman justification for the invasion. Limitation: As William's chaplain he had a clear reason to present William as rightful and Harold as an oath-breaker; English sources tell a different story.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of William of Poitiers, "Gesta Guillelmi" (The Deeds of William), written c. 1071–1077 by William I's chaplain. Limitation: As William's chaplain he had a clear reason to present William as rightful and Harold as an oath-breaker; English sources tell a different story. Award up to [4]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "continuity"?
options: A tax on non-Muslim subjects in some Islamic states, abolished by Akbar in 1564 and restored by Aurangzeb in 1679
The Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires, which used firearms and artillery to build and hold large states
The land revenue system developed by Raja Todar Mal that assessed tax on measured land and average crop yields
Aspects of life that stay the same over a period of time
items.answer: Aspects of life that stay the same over a period of time
items.markingKey: D. "continuity" is aspects of life that stay the same over a period of time.

items.stem: Briefly explain why large medieval empires often broke apart after the death of a strong ruler.
items.answer: Power depended on personal loyalty to the ruler; disputed successions, powerful regional governors and long distances made it hard for weaker heirs to keep control.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Power depended on personal loyalty to the ruler; disputed successions, powerful regional governors and long distances made it hard for weaker heirs to keep control. items.stem: A student claims: "Change in history always means progress." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Change can bring decline as well as improvement – e.g. the collapse of the Mongol khanates or famine after wars.
items.markingKey: Change can bring decline as well as improvement – e.g. the collapse of the Mongol khanates or famine after wars. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the fall of Constantinople in 1453 and explain what it reveals about change in power through new military technology.
items.answer: Mehmed II used giant cannon to breach the city's walls, ending the Byzantine Empire after more than 1 000 years. Gunpowder artillery shifted power to states that could afford it.
items.markingKey: Context (Mehmed II used giant cannon to breach the city's walls, ending the Byzantine Empire after more than 1 000 years.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Briefly explain why gunpowder weapons helped the Ottoman and Mughal empires grow.
items.answer: Expensive cannons and trained musketeers gave rulers who could pay for them a decisive edge over rivals, and artillery broke walls, as at Constantinople in 1453 and at Panipat in 1526.

items.stem: "Between 1200 and 1600 there was more continuity than change in how empires were ruled." Discuss.
items.answer: Mostly continuity in the foundations of power, but important change in the tools of power – armies, bureaucracy and the scale of states.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: hereditary monarchy and religious legitimacy continued in almost all empires; land revenue remained the main source of state income. Supported judgement: Mostly continuity in the foundations of power, but important change in the tools of power – armies, bureaucracy and the scale of states. items.answer: Study the tapestry online (Bayeux Museum); read the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and William of Poitiers extracts; compare events in a table; apply origin, purpose, value and limitation; write conclusions with citations.

items.stem: Explain why "How did labour shortages after the Black Death change the lives of peasants in England between 1348 and 1400?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into feudal society in medieval Europe.
items.answer: It investigates change and causation with a clear period and place, using manor records and secondary studies.
items.markingKey: It investigates change and causation with a clear period and place, using manor records and secondary studies. items.stem:
Source A – Court history (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Abul Fazl, "Akbarnama", written at Akbar's court, c. 1590s

The historian praised the emperor as a wise ruler who treated people of every faith with kindness, listened to the arguments of learned men of all religions and placed justice above everything, so that the land was peaceful and prosperous.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about the Mughal Empire: administration, culture and religion. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Abul Fazl, "Akbarnama", written at Akbar's court, c. 1590s. Purpose: to record and glorify the reign of Akbar for the emperor and his court. Value: It is detailed, written by someone close to the emperor with access to court records, and explains the ideas behind Akbar's policies. Limitation: Abul Fazl was Akbar's friend and official historian, so it presents an idealised picture and omits criticism.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of Abul Fazl, "Akbarnama", written at Akbar's court, c. 1590s. Purpose: to record and glorify the reign of Akbar for the emperor and his court. items.stem: Felix argues that "Between 1200 and 1600 there was more continuity than change in how empires were ruled." Maya disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Mostly continuity in the foundations of power, but important change in the tools of power – armies, bureaucracy and the scale of states.
items.markingKey: Felix: hereditary monarchy and religious legitimacy continued in almost all empires. Maya: gunpowder transformed warfare and the size of states. Judgement (1-2 marks): Mostly continuity in the foundations of power, but important change in the tools of power – armies, bureaucracy and the scale of states.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Historians should rely mainly on primary sources." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Historians need both: primary sources are the evidence, but secondary sources supply context and debate needed to interpret them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they are direct evidence from the time; they show contemporary perspectives and language. Counter-arguments: they are often incomplete, biased or hard to interpret without context; secondary sources bring together many primary sources and expert analysis. Thesis/conclusion: Historians need both: primary sources are the evidence, but secondary sources supply context and debate needed to interpret them. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem:
Source A – Royal charter (paraphrased): Paraphrase of clauses 39 and 40 of Magna Carta, sealed by King John at Runnymede, June 1215

No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land. To no one will we sell, deny or delay right or justice.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "The Black Death was the main reason for the decline of feudalism in England."
items.answer: An important accelerator rather than the only cause: it sped up changes in labour and money rents that had already begun.
items.markingKey: From the source: The king must not punish free men without lawful judgement and must not sell or delay justice. Own knowledge for: labour shortages raised wages and peasants' bargaining power; it led to the Statute of Labourers and the 1381 revolt. Own knowledge against: money rents were already replacing labour services before 1348; the growth of towns, trade and royal government also weakened feudal ties. Judgement: An important accelerator rather than the only cause: it sped up changes in labour and money rents that had already begun. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 3), scaled to the marks: 7-8 thoroughly analyses concepts and issues, summarises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose recognising value and limitations, and clearly recognises different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.answer: Akbar has the strongest claim because his administrative and religious policies created stability that lasted for a century, even if the empire was larger later.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Checking a source against other sources to see whether they agree"?
items.answer: corroboration
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of corroboration.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Magna Carta"?
options: A series of rulers from the same family
A person who received land (a fief) from a lord in return for loyalty and military service
A medieval system in which land was granted in return for loyalty and service, linking the king, nobles, knights and peasants
The charter agreed by King John and his barons in 1215 that limited the king's power and promised justice under the law
items.answer: The charter agreed by King John and his barons in 1215 that limited the king's power and promised justice under the law
items.markingKey: D. "Magna Carta" is the charter agreed by King John and his barons in 1215 that limited the king's power and promised justice under the law.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The empire founded by Babur in 1526 that ruled much of the Indian subcontinent until the 18th century"?
items.answer: Mughal Empire
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of Mughal Empire.

items.stem: Explain why religion was important for the legitimacy of medieval rulers.
items.answer: Rulers claimed to rule by the will of God or as protectors of the faith – crowned by the Pope, as caliph or sultan, or with the support of religious scholars – so obeying them became a religious duty.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rulers claimed to rule by the will of God or as protectors of the faith – crowned by the Pope, as caliph or sultan, or with the support of religious scholars – so obeying them became a religious duty. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Primary sources are always more reliable than secondary sources." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Primary sources can be biased, mistaken or propaganda; reliability depends on origin, purpose and corroboration, not just type.
items.markingKey: Primary sources can be biased, mistaken or propaganda; reliability depends on origin, purpose and corroboration, not just type. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why Magna Carta is seen as important today.
items.answer: It established the idea that the ruler is subject to the law and that free men could not be imprisoned without lawful judgement, an idea later used in constitutional and human-rights documents.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It established the idea that the ruler is subject to the law and that free men could not be imprisoned without lawful judgement, an idea later used in constitutional and human-rights documents. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why Akbar followed a policy of religious tolerance.
items.answer: Most of his subjects were Hindu; tolerance (abolishing jizya, marriage alliances with Rajput families, debates at the Ibadat Khana) won loyalty, reduced revolts and drew talented officials of all faiths into government.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Most of his subjects were Hindu; tolerance (abolishing jizya, marriage alliances with Rajput families, debates at the Ibadat Khana) won loyalty, reduced revolts and drew talented officials of all faiths into government. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Mongol Empire and the Mughal Empire.
items.answer: The Mongol Empire was a vast 13th-century conquest state ruled by nomadic khans that soon split into khanates; the Mughal Empire was a settled, agrarian empire in South Asia with a salaried bureaucracy and a Persianate court that lasted about two centuries.
items.markingKey: The Mongol Empire was a vast 13th-century conquest state ruled by nomadic khans that soon split into khanates; the Mughal Empire was a settled, agrarian empire in South Asia with a salaried bureaucracy and a Persianate court that lasted about two centuries. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why a secondary source may sometimes be more useful than a primary source.
items.answer: A historian writing later can use many primary sources, has hindsight and may be more balanced, so for an overview a secondary source can be more useful.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A historian writing later can use many primary sources, has hindsight and may be more balanced, so for an overview a secondary source can be more useful. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why the mansabdari system strengthened the emperor's control.
items.answer: Every officer's rank, pay and troop numbers were set by the emperor, and postings were transferable, so nobles depended on him rather than on hereditary local power.

items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of clauses 39 and 40 of Magna Carta, sealed by King John at Runnymede, June 1215. Purpose: to make peace between the king and rebel barons by promising to rule according to law. Value: It is the original agreement and shows the limits the barons wanted to place on royal power. Limitation: It was a peace treaty that King John soon rejected, and it protected "free men", not the unfree majority.
